## A software sandcastle

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
![](images/dependency.png){fig-align="center" height="450"}
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
When you write code, you are almost never starting from scratch. Your script *depends* on packages — and those packages depend on other packages. That dependency chain is fragile.

The image to the left, from [XKCD](https://xkcd.com/2347/), captures it perfectly: all of modern infrastructure balancing on a single, unmaintained component.
:::
:::

## Checking what you have installed

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Python

```python
# Check your Python version
import sys
print(sys.version)

# Check a package version
import pandas as pd
print(pd.__version__)
```

```bash
# List all installed packages
pip list

# Show dependencies for a specific package
pip show pandas
```

### R

```r
# Check your R version
R.version.string

# Check a package version
packageVersion("dplyr")

# List all installed packages
installed.packages()[, c("Package", "Version")]

# Show dependencies
tools::package_dependencies("dplyr")
```

:::

::: {.callout-tip}
You can also find package dependencies on [PyPI](https://pypi.org) (Python) and [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org) (R) — look for the *Requirements* or *Imports* section on any package page.
:::

## In practice

::: {.callout-caution}
### Exercises

1.1 What version of Python or R are you running?

1.2 What version of `pandas` (Python) or `dplyr` (R) do you have installed?

1.3 What other packages do you use for your analysis?

1.4 Pick one package from your list — what are its dependencies?
:::
